text: {"decision":"GO","artifact":{"author":"Graham Hill","audience":"Business and IT leaders","perspective":"Business owner only","title":"Valid access is not proof of an authorized payment","reported_facts":[{"text":"CERT-In reports that attackers used valid credentials from victims’ whitelisted infrastructure to invoke fund-transfer APIs directly, bypassing application-level checks. Dummy transaction references had no corresponding records.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046"]},{"text":"The follow-up advisory reports abuse of legitimate cloud management channels, movement from non-production to production through shared credentials or network paths, and attacks after incomplete remediation. It also describes bypassing IP allow-lists through shared third-party fetcher services.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0058"]},{"text":"In a separate incident, Cloudflare reports that credentials stolen in the October 2023 Okta compromise were mistakenly considered unused and left unrotated. Attackers later used them to access its Atlassian environment. Cloudflare reports that segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected.","sources":["CF2024"]}],"inference":{"text":"Previously trusted access stops being reliable evidence of legitimate action when an attacker can reuse the credential, originate traffic through an accepted route, or invoke a sensitive operation without its required business approvals. Successful authentication establishes that an access mechanism accepted the request; it does not, by itself, establish that the underlying payment was authorized. The business decision should therefore depend on evidence linking each payout to an approved obligation, beneficiary and amount.","basis":["CIAD-2026-0046","CIAD-2026-0058","CF2024"]},"business_owner_brief":{"responsibility_status":"Assumption: the business owner has authority over payment operating policy, acceptable disruption and the business conditions for continuing or resuming payouts. Actual accountability must be confirmed locally.","decision_owned":"Determine when payouts may proceed, require additional review or be held, and define the business evidence required before normal processing resumes.","evidence_available":{"reported":"The supplied accounts show that accepted credentials and trusted infrastructure can coexist with unauthorized action. CERT-In recommends matching payouts to approved records, second-level verification, payment-stage limits and reconciliation; these are recommendations, not demonstrated outcomes.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046","CIAD-2026-0058"],"organization_specific":"Assumption: the owner can obtain approved payment records, beneficiary approvals, exception reports and bank or aggregator reconciliation results. None of these organization-specific records was supplied."},"must_learn_from_technical_owner":["Can every route that moves funds enforce the required business validations, including direct API calls and settlement instructions?","Which credentials, execution paths or environments may remain compromised, and what evidence supports eradication and credential replacement?","Can monitoring and retained logs establish what happened, including during low-coverage periods, and what uncertainty remains?"],"hypothetical_illustration":"Assumption-based illustration, not a reported event: a payout arrives with an accepted API credential and an allowed source address, but has no matching approved obligation.
